blocks.text: 13. Converting Audio to MIDI
blocks.raw_html: 13. Converting Audio to MIDI

blocks.text: Although Live’s warping allows for audio files to be used much more flexibly than in traditional audio software, there are also a number of ways to extract musical information from audio clips and place it into MIDI clips, for additional creative possibilities.
blocks.raw_html: Although Live’s warping allows for audio files to be used much more flexibly than in traditional audio software, there are also a number of ways to extract musical information from audio clips and place it into MIDI clips, for additional creative possibilities.

blocks.text: When an audio clip is selected, four conversion commands are available in the Create Menu or the context menu for the clip.
blocks.raw_html: When an audio clip is selected, four conversion commands are available in the Create Menu or the context menu for the clip.

blocks.text: 13.1 Slice to New MIDI Track
blocks.raw_html: 13.1 Slice to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: This command divides the audio into chunks which are assigned to single MIDI notes. Slicing differs from the Convert commands below, in that it doesn’t analyze the musical context of your original audio. Instead, it simply splits the original audio into portions of time, regardless of the content. The Drum Rack provides an ideal environment for working with sliced files, and most of the setup happens automatically after you make a few choices:
blocks.raw_html: This command divides the audio into chunks which are assigned to single MIDI notes. Slicing differs from the Convert commands below, in that it doesn’t analyze the musical context of your original audio. Instead, it simply splits the original audio into portions of time, regardless of the content. The Drum Rack provides an ideal environment for working with sliced files, and most of the setup happens automatically after you make a few choices:

blocks.text: When you select Slice to New MIDI track, you’ll be presented with a dialog box. This offers a list of slicing divisions, as well as a chooser to select the Slicing Preset. The top chooser allows you to slice at a variety of beat resolutions or according to the clip’s transients or Warp Markers. Since a Rack can contain a maximum of 128 chains, Live won’t let you proceed if your choice would result in more than 128 slices. You can fix this by either setting a lower slice resolution or by selecting a smaller region of the clip to slice.
blocks.raw_html: When you select Slice to New MIDI track, you’ll be presented with a dialog box. This offers a list of slicing divisions, as well as a chooser to select the Slicing Preset. The top chooser allows you to slice at a variety of beat resolutions or according to the clip’s transients or Warp Markers. Since a Rack can contain a maximum of 128 chains, Live won’t let you proceed if your choice would result in more than 128 slices. You can fix this by either setting a lower slice resolution or by selecting a smaller region of the clip to slice.

blocks.text: The Slicing Preset chooser contains a few Ableton-supplied slicing templates, as well as any of your own that you may have placed in the Defaults folder in the User Library.
blocks.raw_html: The Slicing Preset chooser contains a few Ableton-supplied slicing templates, as well as any of your own that you may have placed in the Defaults folder in the User Library.

blocks.text: With “Preserve warped timing” enabled, the clip will be sliced in such a way that timing alterations as a result of warping are preserved. With this option disabled, any changes that result from warping will not be reflected in the sliced clip; the sliced version will instead sound like the original, “raw” audio.
blocks.raw_html: With “Preserve warped timing” enabled, the clip will be sliced in such a way that timing alterations as a result of warping are preserved. With this option disabled, any changes that result from warping will not be reflected in the sliced clip; the sliced version will instead sound like the original, “raw” audio.

blocks.text: Once you’ve made your slicing choices and clicked OK, a number of things will happen:
blocks.raw_html: Once you’ve made your slicing choices and clicked OK, a number of things will happen:

blocks.text: A new MIDI track will be created, containing a MIDI clip. The clip will contain one note for each slice, arranged in a chromatic sequence.
blocks.raw_html: • A new MIDI track will be created, containing a MIDI clip. The clip will contain one note for each slice, arranged in a chromatic sequence.

blocks.text: A Drum Rack will be added to the newly created track, containing one chain per slice. Each chain will be triggered by one of the notes from the clip, and will contain a Simpler with the corresponding audio slice loaded.
blocks.raw_html: • A Drum Rack will be added to the newly created track, containing one chain per slice. Each chain will be triggered by one of the notes from the clip, and will contain a Simpler with the corresponding audio slice loaded.

blocks.text: The Drum Rack’s Macro Controls will be pre-assigned to useful parameters for the Simplers, as determined by the settings in the selected slicing preset. In the factory Slicing presets, these include basic envelope controls and parameters to adjust the loop and crossfade properties of each slice. Adjusting one of the Macro Controls will adjust the mapped parameter in each Simpler simultaneously.
blocks.raw_html: • The Drum Rack’s Macro Controls will be pre-assigned to useful parameters for the Simplers, as determined by the settings in the selected slicing preset. In the factory Slicing presets, these include basic envelope controls and parameters to adjust the loop and crossfade properties of each slice. Adjusting one of the Macro Controls will adjust the mapped parameter in each Simpler simultaneously.

blocks.text: Note: Live will take a few moments to process all of this information.
blocks.raw_html: Note: Live will take a few moments to process all of this information.

blocks.text: Playing the MIDI clip will trigger each chain in the Drum Rack in order, according to the timing information that you specified or that was embedded in the audio. This opens up many new editing possibilities, including:

blocks.text: 13.1.1 Resequencing Slices
blocks.raw_html: 13.1.1 Resequencing Slices

blocks.text: By default, your sliced MIDI data will form a chromatically-ascending “staircase“ pattern in order to trigger the correct chains in their original order. But you can create new patterns by simply editing the MIDI notes. You can achieve a similar effect by dragging the Drum Rack’s pads onto each other to swap their note mappings.
blocks.raw_html: By default, your sliced MIDI data will form a chromatically-ascending “staircase“ pattern in order to trigger the correct chains in their original order. But you can create new patterns by simply editing the MIDI notes. You can achieve a similar effect by dragging the Drum Rack’s pads onto each other to swap their note mappings.

blocks.text: 13.1.2 Using Effects on Slices
blocks.raw_html: 13.1.2 Using Effects on Slices

blocks.text: Because each slice lives in its own chain in the Drum Rack, you can easily process individual slices with their own audio effects. To process several slices with the same set of effects, multi-select their chains in the Drum Rack’s chain list and press CtrlG (Win) / CmdG (Mac) to group them to their own nested Rack. Then insert the effects after this new sub-Rack.
blocks.raw_html: Because each slice lives in its own chain in the Drum Rack, you can easily process individual slices with their own audio effects. To process several slices with the same set of effects, multi-select their chains in the Drum Rack’s chain list and press CtrlG (Win) / CmdG (Mac) to group them to their own nested Rack. Then insert the effects after this new sub-Rack.

blocks.text: For even more creative possibilities, try inserting MIDI effects before the Drum Rack. The Arpeggiator and Random devices can yield particularly interesting results.
blocks.raw_html: For even more creative possibilities, try inserting MIDI effects before the Drum Rack. The Arpeggiator and Random devices can yield particularly interesting results.

blocks.text: Slicing is most commonly applied to drum loops, but there’s no reason to stop there. Experiment with slicing audio from different sources, such as voices and ambient textures. The same sorts of resequencing and reprocessing operations can be applied to anything you slice — sometimes with unexpected results.

heading_context.text: 13.2 Convert Harmony to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: This command identifies the pitches in a polyphonic audio recording and places them into a clip on a new MIDI track. The track comes preloaded with an Instrument Rack that plays a piano sound (which can, of course, be replaced by another instrument if you choose).
blocks.raw_html: This command identifies the pitches in a polyphonic audio recording and places them into a clip on a new MIDI track. The track comes preloaded with an Instrument Rack that plays a piano sound (which can, of course, be replaced by another instrument if you choose).

heading_context.text: 13.2 Convert Harmony to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: Note that this command, as with the other Convert commands, differs from slicing in that the generated MIDI clip does not play the original sound, but instead extracts the notes and uses them to play an entirely different sound.
blocks.raw_html: Note that this command, as with the other Convert commands, differs from slicing in that the generated MIDI clip does not play the original sound, but instead extracts the notes and uses them to play an entirely different sound.

heading_context.text: 13.2 Convert Harmony to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: The Convert Harmony command can work with music from your collection, but you can also get great results by generating MIDI from audio recordings of yourself playing harmonic instruments such as guitar or piano.
blocks.raw_html: The Convert Harmony command can work with music from your collection, but you can also get great results by generating MIDI from audio recordings of yourself playing harmonic instruments such as guitar or piano.

heading_context.text: 13.3 Convert Melody to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: This command identifies the pitches in monophonic audio and places them into a clip on a new MIDI track.
blocks.raw_html: This command identifies the pitches in monophonic audio and places them into a clip on a new MIDI track.

heading_context.text: 13.3 Convert Melody to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: The track comes preloaded with an Instrument Rack that plays a synthesizer sound. Using the Rack’s “Synth to Piano” Macro Control, you can adjust the timbre of this sound between an analog-style synth and an electric piano. The instrument was designed to be versatile enough to provide a good preview, but can of course be replaced with another instrument if you choose.

heading_context.text: 13.3 Convert Melody to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: The Convert Melody command can work with music from your collection, but also allows you to record yourself singing, whistling, or playing a solo instrument such as a guitar and use the recording to generate MIDI notes.

heading_context.text: 13.4 Convert Drums to New MIDI Track

heading_context.text: 13.4 Convert Drums to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: This command extracts the rhythms from unpitched, percussive audio and places them into a clip on a new MIDI track. The command also attempts to identify kick, snare and hihat sounds and places them into the new clip so that they play the appropriate sounds in the preloaded Drum Rack.

The command also attempts to identify kick, snare and hihat sounds and places them into the new clip so that they play the appropriate sounds in the preloaded Drum Rack.

heading_context.text: 13.4 Convert Drums to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: As with the Convert Melody command, you can adjust the transient markers in the audio clip prior to conversion to determined where notes will be placed in the converted MIDI clip.
blocks.raw_html: As with the Convert Melody command, you can adjust the transient markers in the audio clip prior to conversion to determined where notes will be placed in the converted MIDI clip.

heading_context.text: 13.4 Convert Drums to New MIDI Track

blocks.text: Convert Drums works well with recorded breakbeats, but also with your own recordings such as beatboxing or tapping on a surface.
blocks.raw_html: Convert Drums works well with recorded breakbeats, but also with your own recordings such as beatboxing or tapping on a surface.

blocks.text: 13.5 Optimizing for Better Conversion Quality
blocks.raw_html: 13.5 Optimizing for Better Conversion Quality

blocks.text: The Convert commands can generate interesting results when used on pre-existing recordings from your collection, but also when used on your own recorded material. For example, you can record yourself singing, playing guitar, or even beatboxing and use the Convert commands to generate MIDI that you can use as a starting point for new music.
blocks.raw_html: The Convert commands can generate interesting results when used on pre-existing recordings from your collection, but also when used on your own recorded material. For example, you can record yourself singing, playing guitar, or even beatboxing and use the Convert commands to generate MIDI that you can use as a starting point for new music.

blocks.text: For the most accurate results, we recommend the following:
blocks.raw_html: For the most accurate results, we recommend the following:

blocks.text: Use music that has clear attacks. Notes that fade in or “swell” may not be detected by the conversion process.
blocks.raw_html: • Use music that has clear attacks. Notes that fade in or “swell” may not be detected by the conversion process.

blocks.text: Work with recordings of isolated instruments. The Convert Drums command, for example, works best with unaccompanied drum breaks; if other instruments are present, their notes will be detected as well.
blocks.raw_html: • Work with recordings of isolated instruments. The Convert Drums command, for example, works best with unaccompanied drum breaks; if other instruments are present, their notes will be detected as well.

blocks.text: Use uncompressed, high-quality audio files such as .wav or .aiff. Lossy data formats such as mp3 may result in unpredictable conversions, unless the recordings are at high bitrates.
blocks.raw_html: • Use uncompressed, high-quality audio files such as .wav or .aiff. Lossy data formats such as mp3 may result in unpredictable conversions, unless the recordings are at high bitrates.

blocks.text: Live uses the transient markers in the original audio clip to determine the divisions between notes in the converted MIDI clip. This means that you can “tune” the results of the conversion by adding, moving, or deleting transient markers in the audio clip before running any of the Convert commands.
blocks.raw_html: Live uses the transient markers in the original audio clip to determine the divisions between notes in the converted MIDI clip. This means that you can “tune” the results of the conversion by adding, moving, or deleting transient markers in the audio clip before running any of the Convert commands.

blocks.text: Although each of the commands has been designed for a particular type of musical material, you can sometimes get very interesting results by applying the “wrong” command. For example, Convert Harmony will usually create chords. So running it on a monophonic clip (like a vocal recording) will often generate notes that weren’t present in the original audio. This can be a great way to spark your creativity.

owner_requirements.title: Command eligibility
owner_requirements.body: Selecting an audio clip exposes Slice and Convert Harmony/Melody/Drums commands in Create or clip context menu. Multi-selection, frozen/group/return/video/take-lane and unsupported source eligibility remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Slicing choices
owner_requirements.body: Slice opens a dialog with beat-resolution, transient or Warp Marker divisions and slicing-preset selection. Slicing partitions source time rather than recognizing pitch. Exact division counting, first/last markers and boundary rounding remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Slicing limit
owner_requirements.body: The slicing workflow prevents proceeding when the chosen plan would exceed128 slices; lower resolution or smaller selected region can reduce the count. This is the slicing-command limit, not a blanket cap on arbitrary rack chains. Exact counting and other eligibility errors remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Slicing presets and warped timing
owner_requirements.body: Slicing presets include supplied templates and user templates from the User Library Defaults folder. Preserve warped timing retains Warp timing changes; disabled follows raw source timing instead. Exact field/default precedence, resampling, fades and audio equality remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Sliced result structure
owner_requirements.body: On successful Slice confirmation a new MIDI track contains a MIDI clip with one chromatically ordered note per slice and a Drum Rack with one chain/Simpler per slice. Each chain responds to its corresponding note and loads the corresponding source region. Starting pitch, note lengths/velocities, media copying and exact reference/boundary representation remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Slicing macros and sequence
owner_requirements.body: Mappings come from the chosen slicing preset; supplied examples include envelope/loop/crossfade controls. A mapped macro adjusts corresponding parameters across the Simplers. Playback triggers slices in original sequence and selected/source timing; exact sample equivalence and processing duration remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Resequencing and per-slice effects
owner_requirements.body: Editing slice notes or swapping rack pad note mappings can reorder playback. Per-chain effects process individual slices; selected chains can be grouped into a nested rack and effects placed after it for shared processing. Generic note/rack operations remain owned by their existing contracts.

owner_requirements.title: Harmony result
owner_requirements.body: Harmony extracts pitched polyphonic content into a new MIDI track/clip with a piano-sound Instrument Rack. It is note recognition and resynthesis, not playback of the original waveform. Exact detected pitches/times/velocities, polyphony and default preset identity are U.

owner_requirements.title: Melody result
owner_requirements.body: Melody targets monophonic pitched audio, creating a new MIDI track/clip with a synthesizer Instrument Rack. Its Synth to Piano macro spans analog-style synth/electric-piano character. Exact detection, macro mapping and preset/DSP identity remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Drums result
owner_requirements.body: Drums extracts unpitched percussive rhythm into a new MIDI track/clip and preloaded Drum Rack, attempting kick/snare/hihat classification. No perfect classifier or exact MIDI key/sample/velocity assignment is promised.

owner_requirements.title: Transient influence and quality
owner_requirements.body: Convert uses source transients for note divisions; changing those markers can alter conversion. Clear isolated attacks and uncompressed audio are recommendations, not guaranteed detection. Wrong-source-class conversion may add notes; reconstruction/precision/recall, onset tie, polyphony and lossy-codec effects remain U.

owner_requirements.title: Recognition algorithms
owner_requirements.body: Pitch/onset/classifier thresholds, tuning/reference pitch, amplitude-to-velocity, overlap/length, silent/ambiguous/invalid source behavior and deterministic repeatability have no finite target oracle here. Retained native task names do not supply a full recognition contract.

owner_requirements.title: Timing and source ownership
owner_requirements.body: Tempo/meter/warp/loop/region/selection changes during processing, source preservation, routing/monitoring, launch ownership, undo grouping, error or cancellation and result placement have no complete oracle.

owner_requirements.title: Files persistence and teardown
owner_requirements.body: Save/reopen, sample copy/collect, missing files, malformed audio/preset, CPU/memory/disk failure, cancellation at progress boundaries and device/Set/application teardown require exact outcomes beyond normal documented creation.
